records.table: Booker's is the barrel proof bourbon Jim Beam bottles uncut and unfiltered, from barrels drawn from the centre of its Kentucky rackhouses. Booker's Bourbon comes in named batches of about six to eight years, each at its own proof: vanilla, oak and brown sugar, hot until water opens it.
records.story: Booker Noe (1929 to 2004), Jim Beam's grandson and for decades the distillery's master distiller, liked his bourbon as it came out of the barrel. For years, as the house tells it, he bottled it uncut and unfiltered from barrels at the centre of the rackhouse and gave it to friends and family at the holidays. Beam dates his introduction of Booker's True Barrel Bourbon to 1987, and most accounts give 1988 for its first general sale. In 1992 Beam gathered it with Baker's, Basil Hayden's and Knob Creek as its Small Batch Bourbon Collection. He laid barrels down to the end: rye he filled in 2003, the year before his death, came out in 2016 as Booker's Rye. Since about 2015 each batch has carried a name, often drawn from his life, his home town of Springfield or his sayings, beside the year and number on the label. Barrel proof is taught from Booker's: one recipe, no water after the barrel, and a strength that changes with every batch, so the label in the hand is the one figure to quote.

records.story: In St. Louis, George T. Stagg (1835 to 1893), a Kentuckian, sold whiskey and bought barrels of O.F.C. bourbon from Colonel E. H. Taylor Jr. When Taylor fell into debt, Stagg took over the O.F.C. distillery in Frankfort in 1878, moving from selling whiskey to making it. In 1904, eleven years after his death, the distillery took his name as the George T. Stagg Distillery. By the distillery's account it was one of six allowed to bottle whiskey for medicine through Prohibition, and Old Stagg became the bourbon it led with as Prohibition ended. The site was renamed Buffalo Trace in 1999, and its Antique Collection began in 2000. George T. Stagg joined the collection in 2002: barrels of the corn led Mash Bill No. 1, left fifteen years and more in new charred oak and bottled uncut and unfiltered in the autumn release. Over those summers each barrel gives more than half its volume to the air, and the strength left behind goes into the bottle, so the proof is written on by hand. George T. Stagg stands at the long end of the barrel proof lesson: the same uncut idea as any batch, carried through fifteen years, and a bottle always poured with a jug of water at hand.

records.story: Behind the name lies the distillery's past: by Buffalo Trace's account, Old Stagg was the bourbon the George T. Stagg Distillery led with as Prohibition ended, and the barrel proof bourbons that carry the name grew from it. George T. Stagg itself had been an autumn release of the Antique Collection since 2002, fifteen years and more in oak. In 2013 Buffalo Trace added a younger bourbon from the same Mash Bill No. 1 and called it Stagg Jr. Its opening batch was drawn from barrels of eight to nine years and bottled uncut and unfiltered, and the distillery meant to release several batches a year rather than one. The batches were numbered as they came, and the fifteenth was released in 2020. In 2022 the Jr. left the label and the bourbon became plain Stagg, its batches marked from then on by the year and a letter, as 22A. Set side by side, the two bottles teach what time does to barrel proof: one recipe, one uncut bottling, about half the years in wood for Stagg, and a proof to read off each batch's label rather than recall.

records.story: Bardstown, where a distillery was founded in 1879, is home to the distillery behind the label. In 2002 it brought out a small batch bourbon named for 1792, the year Kentucky became a state, at first as Ridgewood Reserve 1792. Brown-Forman, the maker of Woodford Reserve, sued over the name and the bottle, a federal judge ruled for it in 2004, and the bourbon became 1792 Ridgemont Reserve, later simply 1792. In 2009 the Sazerac Company bought the distillery and its brands from Constellation Brands, and the site took the name Barton 1792 Distillery. Full Proof followed in 2016. By the brand's account it is bottled at 125 proof, the strength at which its spirit went into new oak, and it skips chill filtering for a plate and frame filter; the launch release came from barrels filled in the autumn of 2007. Reviewers note that the bourbon leaves the barrel stronger and is brought back down to 125, so it is full proof, not barrel proof. The bottle explains the words on a strong label: barrel proof and cask strength mean bottled within two degrees of proof of the strength leaving the barrel, entry proof means the strength going in, and full proof is the house's own name for bottling at entry proof.

records.story: The founder of Barrell Craft Spirits, whose career by the house's account had been in marketing and technology, set the company up in Louisville in 2013. It began as a blender and bottler, not a distiller: it bought aged straight bourbon, chose and married the barrels, and bottled the blend at the strength the barrels gave, without chill filtering, under a batch number. By September 2015 it had reached its fifth bourbon batch, and rye, blended whiskey and rum followed in the same way. The bourbon batches grew more involved as the numbers rose: whiskeys from Tennessee, Kentucky and Indiana in one batch or another, high rye and high corn recipes married together, and a mash bill derived for the whole. In 2024 Batch 036 brought a new label that sets out the states the whiskey came from and the age of each whiskey in the blend. Barrell Bourbon is barrel proof as a blender's choice rather than a distiller's: the strength is the barrels', the recipe is the blend, and the batch number is the bourbon, so a guest is told what this bottle holds and never what an earlier batch held.

quiz.q: In which year was Barrell Craft Spirits founded in Louisville?
quiz.explain: The house dates its founding to 2013; Barrell Whiskey followed in 2015, and 2017 is too late.

sources.title: Barrell Craft Spirits: earlier bourbon batches

report: The plan's note is settled: the founding year, 2013, stands on the house's own About page and on a trade press release; the founder is living and is told by role only. His name and that of the house's former master distiller appeared in sources, and both are added to people.json.

The series is taught, not a batch: the only batch figures given are Batch 038's derived mash bill and tasting notes, from the house's own page, each named as that batch's. The strength range, about 110 to 122 proof, is drawn from batches 001, 024, 025, 031, 037 and 038 as the house's pages and Breaking Bourbon list them.

The class field says straight bourbon whiskey with recent batches blended across states; the exact legal wording on the label for a blend of straight bourbons from several states was not read, and the refuter should check it against 27 CFR 5.143.

Barrell announced in 2017 a distillery of its own in Louisville, and in 2023 opened, and in 2026 sold, a blending and bottling site in Jeffersontown, by trade reports. These are present or recent facts that will age and are left out; whether any Barrell bourbon is now distilled by Barrell was not settled, so the record says it began as a blender.

Left out for want of a source: the make of Batch 001 (a five year Tennessee bourbon at cask strength in one listing and one writer's review, both leads only), and the first year a Barrell Bourbon reached shelves (2013 or 2014 by different accounts).
Barrell Whiskey's start in 2015 rests on Breaking Bourbon's review of Batch 001 and one listing; Gray Label rests on the house's own page. No shelf bottle or Library record exists for Barrell.

changed: bottle.class: under 27 CFR 5.143 a mixture of straight bourbons from different states is a blend of straight bourbon whiskeys, not straight bourbon; the field now says straight bourbon, or a blend of straight bourbon whiskeys where a batch draws on several states, with no talk of recent batches.
bottle.strength: about 110 to 122 proof rested on six batches and does not hold the series; now Varies by batch, cask strength.

bottle.mash and bottle.taste: Batch 038's figures and name were one batch's and not confirmed (Batch 036 reads 79, 16 and 5 in two listings); the mash now says the house derives a mash bill for each batch's label, and the taste gives one batch's notes without its number.

bottle.wood and story: five to sixteen years was in no source for the series, and the front of the label was not confirmed for the ages; now the ages differ by batch and from Batch 036 the label sets them out (The Daily Pour, Breaking Bourbon, the house's release).
story: Barrell Whiskey in 2015 rested on one review; now the fifth bourbon batch by September 2015, the house's own post of that date.

others: Barrell Whiskey's note drops the 2015 Indiana claim for what the house's batch pages show, finishes in other casks; Gray Label Bourbon, a vague tier, gives way to Barrell Seagrass, American and Canadian ryes finished in Martinique rum, apricot brandy and Madeira casks, on the house's own page.
open: bottle.still and the blender card: Barrell planned a distillery of its own; whether any Barrell Bourbon batch is distilled by Barrell was not settled, and the record says it buys aged bourbon.
bottle.mash: whether the derived mash bill sits on the back or the front label was not read off a bottle.
